cards.text: Friend, the Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), has spent a while watching people chase the wind (Ecclesiastes 4:16). Now he walks us up to the house of God. And the first thing he tells us at the door is to guard our steps.

cards.question: At the house of God, the Teacher says to draw near to ___ rather than to offer the sacrifice of fools.
The Teacher says the fools who offer that sacrifice know they are doing wrong.

cards.text: Next he goes after the mouth: don't be quick to speak, and don't rush your heart to say a word before God. Friend, I TALK WITH MY MUSTACHE, so this verse just walked over and sat down right next to me.

cards.question: The Teacher says to let your words be few before God. What reason does he give?

answers.text: God is in heaven and you are on earth
The house of God is always crowded
Short words are easier to remember

cards.text: Then he paints a picture: as a dream comes through many cares. You know the one, friend, that stressed-out week when you dream your boss is a goose running the Monday meeting.

cards.question: In the Teacher's picture, a dream comes through many cares. Whose speech does he say comes with many words?

cards.text: Now the Teacher turns to vows made to God. I promised my oven a clean rack back in March, friend, and that oven has NOT forgotten.

cards.question: The Teacher says that once you make a vow to God, you can take your time fulfilling it.
Don't delay in fulfilling a vow, the Teacher says, because God takes no pleasure in ___.
The Teacher weighs two choices about vows to God. Which does he say is better?

answers.text: Not making a vow at all
Making a vow and not fulfilling it
Making a vow only in private

cards.text: Then comes the warning: don't let your mouth cause your flesh to sin. Your mouth signs up for the job, friend, and the REST of you has to show up Monday morning and do it.

cards.question: The Teacher says not to tell the messenger that your vow was a ___.
The Teacher asks why God should be angry with your words and destroy the work of your hands.

cards.text: He brings the dream picture back one last time: as many dreams bring futility, so do many words. Like that goose-boss dream, friend, a big pile of words goes NOWHERE.

cards.question: After all those warnings about words and vows, what does the Teacher tell us to do?

findings.problem: The question says 'the fools who offer that sacrifice.' 'That sacrifice' points back to card 2, which is no longer on screen. The question should name it, for example 'the fools who offer the sacrifice of fools at the house of God.'

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The joke doesn't share the verse's core action. Verse 2 is about being quick or hasty to speak. Talking with his mustache, which works as his hands, is about gesturing, not about speaking too fast or too much. So 'this verse just walked over and sat down right next to me' doesn't click without explaining.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The right answer stands out. 'God is in heaven and you are on earth' is the only answer that sounds like a reason about God. 'The house of God is always crowded' and 'Short words are easier to remember' sound modern and practical. Both wrong answers should be reasons with the same weight and tone, for example about God's holiness or His patience.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: This true or false card just restates the line of verse 6 and asks whether the Teacher says it. The baker can't reason it out from earlier cards. It tests whether the wording exists, not the movement or the meaning. A better card would ask what is at stake when words go wrong (God's anger, and the work of your hands destroyed) as a meaning question.

rule.text: Ask about the movement and the meaning: what changes, what the picture is, why the speaker says what he says.
